children.text: You can't see all of Egypt in four days. If you choose well, you can read one Egypt in depth.
Egypt is not a country built for short trips.
The pyramids at
Giza
are not a place where you take a photograph and move on. Karnak is not a temple you understand in an hour after lunch. The
Valley of the Kings
is not a place where seeing three tombs is enough.
Cairo
is not a transfer point between the airport and the pyramids.
Even so, many people come to Egypt with only
four days
. Short holidays, layovers, before or after work, a few extra days added to a Red Sea stay. Having only four days doesn't mean the trip has no meaning.
The question is what not to do.
The most dangerous move in a short trip is to try to put a little of everything in: Cairo, Giza,
Luxor
Aswan
Abu Simbel
, the desert,
Alexandria
. Packed into four days, that becomes transport, not travel.
Four days is the length of time for reading one region in depth, or for carefully linking two related ones.
What to decide first
For four days in Egypt, the first decision is not "what do I want to see" but "which Egypt do I want to see."

If you want the symbolic ancient Egypt, the centre is Cairo and Giza. If you want the Valley of the Kings and Karnak, Luxor has to be included. If the southern Nile, the Nubian air, Philae, or Abu Simbel pull at you, the axis is Aswan. If you want landscape more than monuments, the White Desert is an entirely different option.
These are all real trips. They are not the same trip.
Option 1: Stay in Cairo and Giza
For a first trip with only four days, the most honest choice is to stay in Cairo and Giza.
You won't be able to say you saw all of Egypt. But you will see the city of Cairo and the Old Kingdom pyramids without rushing them.

Day 1 is the arrival day. Cairo is large, traffic is heavy, and trying to go to sites the moment you land turns the start of the trip into exhaustion. Check in, eat somewhere nearby, and get used to the sound and the distances of the city. That is enough.
Day 2 goes to
the Giza plateau
. Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure,
the Great Sphinx

, the surrounding cemeteries. If you plan to enter the Great Pyramid, factor in a separate ticket and the time management it requires. Giza reads best in the early morning or the late afternoon. As the angle of the light changes, the surfaces of the stone and the spread of the plateau become legible.

Day 3 goes to the museums and Cairo in layers. The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) holds the complete Tutankhamun collection and Khufu's solar boat, and is one of the most important places to spend time on any current Cairo stay. It deserves a long visit. A different direction is to combine the older Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square,
Coptic Cairo
, the Islamic quarter, the Citadel, and
Khan el-Khalili
Day 4 is the departure day. If the flight time gives you margin, hold it to a short walk or some shopping. Don't underestimate Cairo traffic.
The strength of this shape is that it doesn't push. Pyramids, museum, and the city's history all sit in one place.
Option 2: Link Cairo and Luxor
If you want the two large axes of ancient Egypt in four days, the combination is Cairo and Luxor.

Cairo shows the Old Kingdom and the city in layers. Luxor shows the New Kingdom — the Valley of the Kings, Karnak, the funerary world of the west bank. Short as it is, this is a broad reading of ancient Egyptian history.
It is also a busy trip.
Day 1: arrive in Cairo. Day 2: Giza and the GEM, or Giza and old Cairo. Fly to Luxor in the evening or the next morning.
Day 3 is the west bank in Luxor. Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut,
the Colossi of Memnon
at the centre. If time and energy hold,
Medinet Habu
is worth adding. In the Valley of the Kings, decide which tombs to enter in advance. If you are adding a separate-ticket tomb, don't overload.
Day 4 is the east bank. Karnak in the morning,
Luxor Temple
if possible, and depart in the afternoon or evening.
For four days, this is a strong amount of content. But both Cairo and Luxor really want more time. What you'll see is the outline. Even so, seeing the outline correctly is worth doing.
Option 3: Aswan and Luxor
You can also run a four-day trip that leaves Cairo out and focuses on the Nile valley.
This trip makes the bold choice of not seeing the pyramids. In exchange, time goes to the southern Nile, Aswan, Philae, Luxor, the Valley of the Kings, and Karnak.
Day 1: arrive in Aswan. Depending on arrival time, choose without strain from Philae, the High Dam, and
the Unfinished Obelisk
. Philae is the one that is hardest to leave out — the boat approach to the island carries a quality that is particular to Aswan.

Day 2: choose between Abu Simbel and a deeper Aswan day. Abu Simbel is a powerful experience, but the travel is long. A day in Aswan can combine the Nubian Museum, Elephantine Island, a felucca, and the local markets.
Day 3: travel to Luxor, with Luxor Temple in the evening. Day 4: focus the day on the Valley of the Kings and Karnak.
As a Nile trip, this is a beautiful shape. Short as it is, the southward-to-Thebes movement still emerges. The transfers have to be designed carefully, or four days starts to feel cramped.
Option 4: Cairo and Alexandria
For travellers who want a Mediterranean Egypt in addition to ancient Egypt, there is the Cairo and Alexandria combination.

Alexandria has a face that is entirely different from Giza or Luxor. Founded by Alexander, made the Ptolemaic capital, it was the centre of Mediterranean learning and trade. Its ancient remains today are fragmentary, but they are interesting fragments.

The catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa show a distinctive funerary culture that mixed Egyptian, Greek, and Roman imagery. The Qaitbay Fortress stands where the ancient Pharos Lighthouse once stood. The new Bibliotheca Alexandrina is not an archaeological site, but it is a modern institution that takes up the memory of knowledge this city has carried.
In four days, the shape is: two days in Cairo, one day in Alexandria, one day for departure. It suits travellers who want to keep Giza and the GEM in but also add the Mediterranean contrast.
Option 5: The White Desert
For people who have already seen the pyramids and Luxor, or for travellers who want landscape more than monuments, the White Desert is an option.

Bahariya Oasis lies southwest of Cairo. From there the route runs to the Black Desert, Crystal Mountain, and the White Desert. In the White Desert, wind-carved white chalk forms spread across the floor, and at night the sky opens widely.
This is not a trip of ancient temples. It is a way of seeing Egypt through geology and quiet.

A four-day White Desert trip needs a vehicle and a reliable guide. It suits travellers who don't mind camping in the desert and longer drives. For a first Egypt trip without the pyramids in it, this isn't the highest-priority choice. For a second or later trip, it is a very strong one.
Option 6: Abu Simbel and Nubia
A four-day trip can also be built around Abu Simbel.

The Great Temple of Ramses II and the smaller temple dedicated to Nefertari sit south of Aswan, near Lake Nasser. In the 1960s, to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser, the temples were cut apart and moved to higher ground. That rescue work was one of the great moments of modern archaeology and of international cooperation.

Abu Simbel alone can be done as a day trip. With four days, however, you can combine it with Aswan, Philae, the Nubian Museum, and in some cases the temples around Lake Nasser, and the trip resolves into a southern Egypt route.
This is a trip you choose instead of Cairo and Giza. It is not the most common shape for a first Egypt trip, but it has meaning for travellers who feel strongly drawn to the south.
How to choose
The most important thing in four days in Egypt is to set the right expectations.
For a first visit that wants the symbolic Egypt, Cairo and Giza is the most stable.
For seeing the two great periods of ancient Egypt, Cairo and Luxor.
For the southern Nile and the temples, Aswan and Luxor.
For a different, Mediterranean Egypt, add Alexandria.
For a second or later trip looking for quiet and landscape, the White Desert.
For Nubia and the southern monuments of Ramses II, Abu Simbel at the centre.
Each works as a four-day trip. What doesn't work is trying to mix all of them into one.
Practical notes
In a four-day trip, the design of the transfers determines the quality.

Cairo to Luxor by air is about an hour. Cairo to Aswan, about 90 minutes. With airport transfers, check-in, and wait times, a flight day costs you half a day. If you have a domestic flight, don't load that day with too many sites.
October to April is the easier season. December and January are crowded. May to September is hot, and in Luxor, Aswan, and Abu Simbel the schedule has to be built around the early morning.

You don't need a guide everywhere. But at the Valley of the Kings, Karnak, the GEM, and Giza, a knowledgeable guide changes how much you understand. The shorter the trip, the more a good guide matters — there isn't time to do your own research on the ground.
In a short trip, it is also important to avoid unnecessary souvenir shops and over-long meal breaks. Time is limited. In four days, what you don't spend time on is part of the itinerary.
What four days gives you
You can't finish understanding Egypt in four days.
You can find one doorway into Egypt in four days.

In Cairo, the city in layers and the scale of the Old Kingdom. In Luxor, kingship and the world after death. In Aswan, the southern Nile and the air of Nubia. In the White Desert, the silence of an Egypt without monuments. In Alexandria, a different history that opened onto the Mediterranean.
What makes a short trip bad is not the shortness itself.
What makes it bad is trying to push the whole country into a short time.
If you have four days, choose one Egypt. With that decision made clearly, a short trip doesn't have to be shallow.

deck: Four days in Egypt is not enough time to circle the country. Which Egypt you choose — Cairo, Luxor, Aswan, or the desert — changes what the trip means.
